Since this is voat, let's talk about voting systems! America uses a vote-for-one voting system that prevents new ideas and candidates from entering the national discussion. Game theory predicts that a vote-for-one voting system eventually turns into in a two party system. Here is an illustration of how that happens

But it doesn't have to be this way!

The necessary requirement to fix our voting system is to allow voters to express their opinion on more than one candidate.

How do we do that?

The simplest way is to allow voters to vote for all of the candidates they support. This should sound familiar because it's the same system used by the Olympics, but on a scale of 0-1.

The technical name for this system is Approval Voting, and it's how America will move forward as a country.

Thoughts?

I would think that while it is true that a first-past-the-post election pulls discussion toward the center, the primaries that come before can pull in all sorts of directions. There have definitely been many presidential and gubernatorial elections with such outcomes like in 1964 for example. For congressmen or elections in a Westminster system like in the UK or Canada where the MPs elect the executive branch (the Prime Minister), this is very different, but for executive branch elections here, I disagree that first-past-the-post prevents new ideas and candidates from entering the national discussion.
Hotelling's model, "The tendency of the outermost entrepreneur to approach the cluster" accurately predicts the policy drift of a candidate during primary and general elections.

Approval voting along with either getting rid of "winner takes all" states or even direct popular voting will be good I think. It even gets rid of battleground states so everyone's vote becomes more important.

Approval voting is really the complement of something like vote-with-instant-runoff. Their benefits and issues are mirror each other. Here's an example of how approval voting could go wrong.

If a majority of voters have a preference for candidate A over B, there's no guarantee B beats A. Lets say 51% of the population would rather have A than B, but approve of both. 49% of the population approves only of B. Candidate B gets elected with 100% approval. It would have been in the best interests of the people preferring Candidate A to lie on their ballot, saying they only approve of their preferred candidate. This basically the opposite of the "avoid the third party candidate" problem majority voting has.

(I took the Coursera course that covers voting and this is the first time I've gotten a chance to discuss it, check it out if this stuff interests you).

Approval Voting requires strategic voting on the behalf of the voter (as does the current vote-for-one system), and so it is incorrect to ignore polling data and strategic voting in your example. This is why Approval Voting performs poorly in organizational election like the Dartmouth Board of Trustees where there was no polling data, but would perform well in political elections where there is polling data.

Approval voting isn't a step in the right direction because it doesn't lead to a better result necessarily. If we have Candidate A, who is the most popular but also the most controversial, Candidate B who is the second strongest candidate but less popular, and Candidate C, who is mediocre but is safe from the perspectives of A and B; then Candidate C would win an election under approval voting, even if Candidate A has 51% support for the simple reason that everyone who supports A and B has an incentive to vote also for C because they don't want the other to win. Instant Runoff Voting is a far better system for a FPTP election.

Approval voting satisfies the necessary criteria that a voting method needs to allow voters the opportunity to express their opinion about more than one candidate in order to eliminate vote splitting. In terms of information gathered in an election with n candidates, plurality voting gathers 1 bit of information, approval voting gathers n bits of information, and ranked preference gathers n! bits of information. In that regard, Approval Voting is a step in the right direction.

If we have Candidate A, who is the most popular but also the most controversial, Candidate B who is the second strongest candidate but less popular, and Candidate C, who is mediocre but is safe from the perspectives of A and B; then Candidate C would win an election under approval voting, even if Candidate A has 51% support for the simple reason that everyone who supports A and B has an incentive to vote also for C because they don't want the other to win. Instant Runoff Voting is a far better system for a FPTP election.

Some would argue that a compromise candidate elected by 80% is better than a condorcet candidate with 51%. Regardless, you have overlooked an important facet of elections, and that is strategic voting. Approval Voting has famously failed in situations where voters did not have sufficient polling data to strategically vote (See Approval Voting and the Dartmouth Board of Trustees). When given polling data, voters are able to make an informed decision on who they should strategically vote for.

I am not saying that Approval Voting is better than Ranked Preference, but Approval Voting does hold a special place in voting systems as the simplest voting method that effectively eliminates the spoiler effect. Some of my favorite voting systems are Mixed Member Proportional, and the Schulze Method. They are amazing voting systems, but they do suffer from complexity. That's why I consider Approval Voting as a good first step towards fixing the American Voting system.

Strategic voting in any system is a flaw, since ideally the system should reflect people's genuine preferences. And technically speaking, proportional representation is the only system that satisfies Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (i.e., non-dictatorship, independence of irrelevant alternatives, Pareto efficiency with respect to the election outcome). The closest FPTP system is Instant-Runoff, which only violates Independence of Irrelevant alternatives by the comparatively rare phenomenon of the excluded middle. Approval voting on the other hand violates both Independence of Irrelevant alternatives, since a third party can screw up the election (for example, candidate A is socialist, candidate B a conservative, and candidate D a fascist. Say under these conditions candidate B wins. If you have a social liberal running as candidate D, and A votes for D because they don't want B and B votes for it because they don't want C, then D will win); it also violates Pareto Efficiency since in the example given in the other post despite Group X preferring Candidate Y, approval voting is capable of yielding an election in which Candidate Z is elected.

Finally, if your concern is with fixing the American political system, approval voting won't do anything, since given a choice between the Left, the Democrats, and the Republicans, the Republicans and Democrats will still win because Approval voting relies on electing the lesser evil, so it still doesn't solve the problem of Duverger's Law. And anyway, since the two parties in particular and the capitalist class in general will do nothing to weaken their power without coercion, you may as well advocate the best possible system rather then what's easy to do.

Strategic voting in any system is a flaw

It has been shown by the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem that, if a voting method for choosing one of several options is completely strategy-free, then it must be either dictatorial or nondeterministic.
Which is why I said ideally. Hence the closest to a non-strategic system is best.

FYI, Approval Voting does not fall under Arrow's Impossibility Theorem because it is not a ranked order voting system.
